newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. soybean sales to China not confirmed - traders.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soybean sales to China not confirmed - traders.

text.p: Hong Kong and China grains traders on Monday said they could not confirm U.S. soybean sales to China but added that while U.S. beans were more expensive than South American beans, a U.S. deal was not inconceivable.
"We're still trying to confirm it, but nothing so far," said one Hong Kong grains trader.

Chicago Board of Trade soybean futures jumped on Friday on talk China had purchased at least one cargo of U.S. soybeans and possibly two more for May/June delivery, helping to push May soybeans up 20-3/4 to $8.67-3/4 per bushel.
Hong Kong traders said the gap between China's domestic soybean price and international prices was narrower and imports were possible but that profit margins were negligible.

"We don't see the kinds of margins to justify the transactions," said one China-based source, noting that last year the difference in domestic and international prices allowed profits in the range of 200 yuan ($24) per tonne.

Domestic soybean prices currently ranged between 3,100 and 3,200 yuan per tonne, while imported soybeans would cost around 3,500 yuan per tonne, including the 13 percent value-added tax (VAT), sources said.
"It is possible that an end-user has licences and does not have to pay the VAT, in which case (U.S.) imports might be possible," said one trader.
South American soybeans were still cheaper than U.S. soybeans, dealers said.
U.S. beans were quoted at around US$350 per tonne, C&F China, on Monday while South American beans were around $5 to $10 cheaper, sources said.
Traders had not heard of soybean import licences being issued, but noted that price usually weighed heavier than licence availability in China's buying decisions.
"As long as the price is right, people will find ways of getting the stuff in," said one source.
Demand in China for both soybeans and meal was healthy, dealers said.
"We feel that last year the crop wasn't very good. There is a need for both beans and meal," another China-based source noted.
This year's crop planting had already begun in some areas and harvesting, expected to take place later in September, would likely drive soybean prices down, traders said.
"Last year, at the Dalian Commodities Exchange the highest price of soybeans was 3,400 yuan and it dropped to around 2,900 yuan per tonne after the harvest," one source noted.
